title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
trick: Tell the agent a turn cap, stop it there, and call a task's depth the smallest cap under which it still passes; 94% of solved synthetic 'long-horizon' terminal tasks pass within three.
framing_stripped: Called 'measuring and synthesizing depth in terminal tasks' with two quantities 'used in parallel computing, its work and its depth' (Blelloch, sec. 1) and a pipeline named Depth ('Derives Each segment of a task by Performing and Testing it in a real software environment, Handing the state it leaves to the next segment', sec. 1); it is (a) a turn-capped re-run of 734 sampled tasks from six terminal-task datasets (TMax, FACET, SETA, RST synthetic; Terminal-Bench 2.0 and TerminalWorld-Verified human-curated) by two cheap models (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) in the terminus-2 harness under caps $\{1,2,3,5,10,20,40,80\}$, recording per task the smallest cap that passes ($D$) and the lines of the reference solution ($W$); (b) the finding that 278 of the 296 solved synthetic tasks (94%) pass within three turns, that the turn count $N$ a model takes without a cap is several times $D$ (TMax reports 16.3 mean turns, median $D$ of its solved tasks 1; Table 1), and that $D$ predicts public pass rates once $W$ is controlled (rank partial correlation $-0.31$ on 105 solved TB2 and TW tasks) while $N$ does not ($+0.06$; sec. 4.3); (c) an LLM generation agent that, inside a Docker environment drawn from TerminalWorld packages, writes a 3-6 segment task one segment at a time, doing each segment before writing its solution and checks, so that each segment has a 'key step' where the usual command fails and the next segment needs what the key step produced (sec. 3.3-3.4); 105 such tasks, 54 solved by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 44 of those with $D \geq 40$, pass@1 17-47% across six models, frontier models under 50% (Table 2); and (d) SFT of Qwen3-8B on 4,941 samples from 1,272 runs, pass@1 2.6% to 4.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 3.4% to 9.1% on OpenThoughts-TBLite (sec. 4.6). The headline is the audit; the pipeline and the SFT are the recipe consequence.
method_equations: Task (sec. 2): $\tau = (I, e_0, \sigma, V)$ in the Harbor format, with instruction $I$, initial Docker state $e_0$, reference shell script $\sigma$ and verifier $V$; multi-segment form $I = (I_1, \dots, I_k)$, likewise $\sigma$ and $V$, delivered one at a time in one container. Segment $s$ passes on state $e$ if $$V_s(e) = \prod_{c \in V_s} c(e) = 1,$$ where each check $c$ maps a state to $\{0, 1\}$. Runs: in turn $t$ the agent writes one reply with a batch of commands $a_t$ (possibly a script with branches and loops), the harness returns the output $o_t$; a run $(a_1, o_1, \dots, a_n, o_n)$ has $n$ turns over all segments; with $\hat{e}_s$ the state at the end of segment $s$ ($V_s(\hat{e}_s) = 0$ if the run stops earlier) a run passes if $$R = \prod_{s=1}^{k} V_s(\hat{e}_s) = 1.$$ Turn-capped evaluation with cap $T$: the agent is told at most $T$ turns are available and the harness stops after turn $T$, so $n \leq T$. Idealized depth (eq. 3): a strategy $\pi$ chooses $a_t = \pi(I_1, \dots, I_s, o_1, \dots, o_{t-1})$; $n_\pi(e)$ is the number of turns $\pi$ needs to pass from initial state $e$ ($\infty$ if never); $\mathcal{E}(\tau)$ is the set of initial states that differ from $e_0$ only in details the instruction leaves open (file contents, versions, defaults) and that $\sigma$ solves once adapted; then $$D^{*} = \min_{\pi} \max_{e \in \mathcal{E}(\tau)} n_\pi(e),$$ 'the fewest turns that suffice whichever state in $\mathcal{E}(\tau)$ the agent faces' (sec. 2) — rounds of interaction, as in adaptive complexity, not dependencies between operations: a dependency a batch can resolve by branching on its own output adds no turn; 'a step that depends on an output it could not anticipate, such as an unfamiliar error or code to be patched, needs a turn of its own' (sec. 2). Idealized work (eq. 4): with $\mathcal{A}$ the set of command sequences that pass from a known $e_0$ with harness limits lifted ($\sigma \in \mathcal{A}$), $$W^{*} = \min_{a \in \mathcal{A}} |a|,$$ $|a|$ counting lines, one command per line and each written line of file content separately, summed over segments; $W^{*}$ is taken at $e_0$ alone so 'the cost of not knowing the state falls entirely on $D^{*}$' (sec. 2). Estimates (eqs. 5-6, sec. 3.1): caps $\mathcal{T} = \{1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80\}$; for model $m$, $P^m_T = 1$ if $m$ passes the task under cap $T$ (in at least one of up to two runs, App. B); $$D_m = \min\{T \in \mathcal{T} : P^m_T = 1\}, \qquad D = \min_{m \in \mathcal{M}} D_m,$$ over the models that give an estimate; $\mathcal{M} = \{$DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash$\}$; a task passed only without a cap is recorded as $> 80$, a task never passed gives no estimate. $W$ = non-blank, non-comment lines of $\sigma$ summed over segments (TMax releases no $\sigma$, so its $W$ counts the lines of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's passing commands at its smallest passing cap, App. D). Whose behaviour $D$ depends on: the paper's own statement is 'Unlike the idealized $D^{*}$, $D$ depends on the models, the harness and the single state $e_0$, so it is an estimate rather than a bound' (sec. 2). The model's: $D$ is a min over models because 'a model that merges poorly overestimates the depth' (sec. 3.1), and the two models were chosen by calibration tasks in which ten parallel or statically chained steps pass under cap 3 while a chain whose step $i$ is encrypted with the answer to step $i-1$ does not (App. B); adding GLM-5.3-Flash lowers $D$ on 40 of the 160 existing tasks it was run on (32 by one cap) and on 4 of 54 of the paper's own (App. E.1). The cap's: the cap is text appended to the instruction ('Plan for this limit: batch commands where you can, and do not spend turns on steps that are not needed', App. B), the harness stops the run after turn $T$, outputs are cut to 10,000 bytes and a command is waited for at most 60 s per turn (App. B), and in multi-segment tasks the cap covers all segments. The task's: only through $e_0$, not the set $\mathcal{E}(\tau)$. Run protocol (App. B): DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash first runs twice without a cap (150-turn limit); if neither passes there is no estimate; $N_m$ is its fewest passing turns; 'Caps at or above $N_m$ count as passed without being run'; caps below $N_m$ are tried in increasing order with up to two runs each; GLM-5.3-Flash 'runs only at the caps below the estimate of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash' and 'can therefore only lower $D$'. Pipeline (sec. 3.3-3.4): the generation agent plans a goal in $k$ segments; for segment $s$ it writes $I_s$, carries the segment out, then writes $\sigma_s$ and $V_s$; a clean container replays $e_s = \sigma_s(e_{s-1})$. Each segment has a key step, 'a step where the usual way of doing it goes wrong in this environment, with an error or silently, and only running the commands reveals it'; $\tilde{\sigma}_s$ is $\sigma_s$ with its key step removed; with $\mathrm{res}(e)$ the results (files, accounts, configuration) holding in $e$, segment $s + 1$ must use a result in $$R_s = \mathrm{res}(e_s) \setminus \mathrm{res}\bigl(\tilde{\sigma}_s(e_{s-1})\bigr), \qquad s < k,$$ (eq. 7) and the last segment preserves earlier results, $\mathrm{res}(e_{k-1}) \subseteq \mathrm{res}(e_k)$. Verifier rules (eq. 8): $V_s(e_{s-1}) = 0$ and $V_s(\tilde{\sigma}_s(e_{s-1})) = 0$; every name a check relies on appears verbatim in $I_s$, the fix of the key step does not. Acceptance (eq. 9): replay of $\sigma$ from $e_0$ in a fresh offline container gives $V_s(e_s) = 1$ for all $s$. Audit numbers (Table 1; sampled / solved, solved = DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash passes at least one of two uncapped runs): TMax 100 / 94, FACET 210 / 53, SETA 100 / 91, RST 200 / 58, TB2 39 / 37, TW 85 / 68; 734 sampled, 401 solved (296 synthetic, 105 human-curated); ours 105 / 54. Share of solved tasks with $D \leq 3$: 100%, 92%, 98%, 79%, 89%, 90%, ours 0%; with $D \geq 5$: 0%, 8%, 2%, 21%, 11%, 10%, ours 100%. Medians over solved tasks, $D$ / $N$ / $W$: TMax 1 / 5 / 58, FACET 2 / 7 / 204, SETA 1 / 5 / 25, RST 2 / 7 / 119, TB2 1 / 8 / 44, TW 1 / 9 / 11, ours 40 / 45 / 315; mean $N$ 5.8 to 11.6 existing, 52.8 ours; end-of-run context tokens (thousands, mean) 6.6 to 19.3 existing, 67.0 ours. Reported mean turns in the original papers: TMax 16.3, FACET 11.86. 'Of the 296 solved synthetic tasks, 278 (94%) have $D \leq 3$' (sec. 4.2); in TMax and SETA nearly nine in ten have $D = 1$; on the 88 solved TMax tasks with released Gemini runs, Gemini takes a median of 8 turns while median $D$ is 1; '96 of the 170 tasks with $N$ between 6 and 10 have $D = 1$'; median $W$ 68 lines synthetic vs 17 human-curated while the $D \geq 5$ share 'is no higher for the synthetic datasets (6% versus 10%)'; '11 of their 105 solved tasks have $D \geq 5$' (human-curated). Depth vs difficulty (sec. 4.3; Figure 4): rank partial correlation (ranks, then correlate two variables after removing the linear effect of a third) of the public pass rate (TB2: mean over 15 leaderboard submissions; TW: share of eight models solving the task) with $D$ controlling for $W$: $-0.31$ on 105 solved TB2 + TW tasks, $-0.49$ on TB2 alone; on the paper's own tasks, pass rate = mean of GLM-5.3-Flash, GPT-6 Luna, MiMo-V2.6-Flash and GPT-6.1 Sol, $D$ from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash alone, $-0.29$ (95% CI $-0.53$ to $-0.02$) over 52 solved tasks with results from all four; pooled $-0.31$. $N$ controlling for $D$ vs public pass rate: $+0.06$ (95% CI $-0.18$ to $+0.26$). Generation-time difficulty labels vs released pass rates: $-0.07$ to $-0.11$ (TW task-file labels: none), TB2 author ratings $-0.46$ (Figure 8, all tasks with released pass rates). TB2 author rating vs $D$ controlling for $W$: $+0.55$ (95% CI $+0.29$ to $+0.75$) on 37 solved tasks; 9 of 11 sampled tasks rated hard have $D \geq 2$ vs 8 of 28 rated easy or medium; $W$ and $N$ vs rating controlling for $D$: $+0.16$ and $-0.28$, CIs containing zero. Splitting TB2 + TW at $D = 2$ and median $W$: tasks large in both have mean within-dataset pass-rate percentile 0.29 vs 0.53-0.59 for the other three groups. Robustness (App. E.2): on tasks with $R = 1$ (both uncapped runs pass) the correlations are $-0.43$, $-0.39$, $-0.40$ (human-curated, ours, pooled); 95% of synthetic tasks $D \leq 3$. Own tasks (sec. 4.4; App. G, H): 98 of 105 have six segments, 4 five, 3 three; of the 54 solved, 2 have $D = 10$, 8 $D = 20$, 23 $D = 40$, 17 $D = 80$, 4 not passed within 80 turns; merging all segments into one instruction on 25 random solved tasks (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash alone, caps tried downward from the original $D$): $D$ does not decrease for 17 of 25 (68%) — '8 pass at the original cap and 9 are not solved within it' — 7 drop one cap level, 1 two; against the original task of the same seed environment (35 pairs) the original has $D \leq 10$ in 34 and $D = 1$ in 26, ours $D \geq 20$ and higher in all 35 (sign test $p = 5.8 \times 10^{-11}$). Replays with parts removed (Table 8; counts over segments): $V_s$ fails on $e_{s-1}$ in 601 / 602 (99.8%), with the previous segment skipped 462 / 501 (92.2%), with one event removed 158 / 165 (95.8%), with the key step removed 598 / 604 (99.0%), and $V_{s+1}$ fails after the key step of $s$ is removed in 421 / 500 (84.2%). Cost: $113.66 for 136 seed environments, 105 accepted (77%), about $1.08 per accepted task, excluding evaluation and the measurement of $D$. Model evaluation (Table 2; two uncapped runs per task, a run stops at the first failed segment; pass@1 averaged within task then over tasks): Claude Sonnet 5.5 (effort high) 47%, segments 0.70; GPT-6.1 Sol (medium) 44%, 0.69; GPT-6 Luna (medium) 20%, 0.43; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (high) 40%, 0.64; MiMo-V2.6-Flash 30%, 0.50; GLM-5.3-Flash (max) 17%, 0.38; of 90 tasks with results from all six, 29 passed by none; geometric-mean conditional per-segment pass 0.88 (Claude) to 0.74 (GLM), share passing all six segments 47% vs 16%. Refusals (App. I): GPT-6.1 Sol refused 7 tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 refused 12 and returned empty on 3; 'A task without a valid result is left out of the denominator of that model'. Fine-tuning (sec. 4.6; App. J): Qwen3-8B non-thinking, 4,941 samples from 1,272 uncapped runs of the six models, segments kept while passing in a row, runs cut where terminus-2 would compress the context and the next sample started from the summary and Q&A; TB2.1 pass@1 2.6% to 4.9%, TBLite 3.4% to 9.1%, three runs per task, bars with one standard deviation (Figure 7); hyperparameters unknown (not in text).
load_bearing_assumption: That a strong model told the cap passes at the smallest cap the task permits, so the first cap at which one of two runs passes measures the task and not the model: 'A model used to measure depth must merge commands into fewer turns once told the cap; otherwise it measures work' (App. B). The evidence for the two chosen models is three calibration families (ten parallel steps, ten statically chained steps, a six-step chain encrypted step by step) under cap 3 plus three TMax tasks under cap 1 (App. B); on real tasks the second model lowered $D$ on 40 of 160 (25%), so a third stronger merger would lower it again by an unknown amount. If a run's failure at a cap is caused by planning limits, run-to-run noise or the 10,000-byte output truncation rather than by a round the task forces, $D$ is a model property and 'depth predicts difficulty' is partly 'the model that measured $D$ fails where other models fail' — the paper names this ('this error could produce a correlation between $D$ and difficulty that does not come from depth', App. E.2) and answers it only with the $R = 1$ subset. Second: that non-blank lines of the reference solution are the right 'work' to control for when claiming depth predicts difficulty beyond work; $W$ is one author's script ('lines depend on coding style', App. D; Spearman 0.98 with BPE tokens over 739 tasks), not $W^{*} = \min_{a} |a|$. Third, for the audit's generality: that the sampled tasks represent their datasets although 'Only tasks that at least one model passes in the released results are drawn' (App. C) and only solved tasks get a $D$; the paper reweights the $D \geq 5$ share to original label proportions (SETA 2.2% to 1.5%, RST 20.7% to 14.9%, TB2 10.8% to 11.9%, TW 10.3% to 11.8%; Table 5) but the never-passed tail is absent by construction.
weakest_component: The estimator $D$ itself, and its censoring. (1) 333 of the 734 sampled tasks are not solved by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and get no $D$ (401 solved; Table 1), after a sampling rule that already drew 'Only tasks that at least one model passes in the released results' (App. C; 'in the hardest level of TMax, only 1 of the 59 tasks with released Gemini runs was ever passed'); the deep tail, where the claim 'synthesis adds work rather than depth' matters most, is where the instrument is blank — FACET keeps 53 of 210, RST 58 of 200. (2) The cap grid $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80\}$ doubles above 5, so '$D = 40$' means 'failed twice at 20, passed once at 40'; 44 of the paper's 54 solved tasks sit at 40, 80 or above, where one cap level is a factor of two, and the merged-instruction test (App. H) counts 9 tasks 'not solved within' the original cap as 'does not decrease', which is censoring, not evidence of equal depth. (3) Up to two runs per cap and 'Caps at or above $N_m$ count as passed without being run' (App. B): a task that passes rarely has its $D$ inflated by failed runs, and those tasks are the hard ones (App. E.2; the authors decline to control for $R$: 'a deep task has many steps that can each go wrong, so part of the variation in $R$ may come from depth itself'). (4) The second model only runs below the first model's estimate and only on tasks with $D > 1$, so the min in eq. 6 is one-sided by design ('It can therefore only lower $D$'), and the paper's own robustness check says a single model would make the existing sets look deeper (App. E.1); the direction of the bias from adding a better merger is known, its size is not. (5) The 'depth predicts difficulty' result is rank partial correlation on 105 (TB2 + TW) and 52 (own) tasks with the own-task CI reaching $-0.02$; on the own tasks the pass-rate average includes models of different effort settings and a model refused on 15 tasks. (6) The harness is not the datasets' harness: a 30-minute agent time limit replaces each dataset's own, 'shorter for 66, mostly SETA tasks with 60 minutes' (App. B); TMax and SETA are audited under terminus-2 although they trained and reported under other harnesses (Table 3). (7) The SFT result is on an 8B model at 2.6-9.1% pass@1 with three runs; no comparison to SFT on an equal number of samples from the audited shallow datasets, so 'depth helps training' is not isolated from 'more and longer trajectories help'.
regime: Measurement models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash (TB2.1 scores 90.6 and 84.3 as reported by their developers; $0.30 / $1.20 and $0.15 / $0.50 per million input / output tokens; App. B), both in terminus-2; caps $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80\}$, up to two runs per cap, 150-turn limit without a cap, agent time limit 30 minutes on existing tasks and 3 hours (2.5 / 1.5 for five- / three-segment) on the paper's own, outputs cut to 10,000 bytes keeping first and last 5,000, per-command wait at most 60 s (App. B). Audited: 734 sampled tasks from six datasets (TMax 100, FACET 210, SETA 100, RST 200, TB2 39, TW 85), 401 solved, excluding tasks needing GPUs, privileged containers, downloads over 200 MB or builds over 1 GB / 10 minutes (App. C); run lengths on solved existing tasks 5-9 median turns, 0.8-2.2 minutes, 6.6-19.3 thousand end-of-run tokens (Table 1). Own tasks: 105, from 136 seed environments drawn mostly from the 1,530 TerminalWorld packages, 3-6 segments (98 with six), median 330 lines of reference solution and 1,406 instruction words per task (Table 9); categories software engineering 18, environment setup 17, system administration 16, security 15, 18 other categories 35, unlabeled 4 (App. G); no network access during generation or evaluation. Evaluated: six models, two uncapped runs each, pass@1 17-47%, mean segments 0.38-0.70, 26-48 turns and 29-58.5 thousand tokens per run (Table 2); GPT-6 Luna at effort medium, others at provider defaults; open-weight models and GPT-6 Luna via OpenRouter with fixed providers, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 via TokenRouter (App. I). Training: Qwen3-8B, SFT, non-thinking mode, 4,941 samples from 1,272 runs; evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and OpenThoughts-TBLite, three runs per task, pass@1 2.6% to 4.9% and 3.4% to 9.1% (sec. 4.6). Generation cost $113.66 for 136 environments (sec. 4.4). Code and Dataset link labels appear in the header; URLs, venue, SFT hyperparameters and the generation agent's model: unknown (not in text). arXiv v1, 1 Nov 2026, cs.AI.
information_asymmetry: The ruler runs at evaluation time and reads one bit per (model, cap): did a run pass. From that bit it cannot separate a round the task forces (an output no reply could anticipate) from a round the model spent because it did not merge, a round spent waiting for a slow command or reading a truncated output, or a failed run at a sufficient cap; the paper says so ('$D$ depends on the models, the harness and the single state $e_0$', sec. 2) and bounds the model part only from one side (a second model lowers $D$ on 25% of existing tasks, App. E.1). At task-construction time the paper holds exactly the information the estimate lacks, for its own 105 tasks: the generation agent knows per segment which step is the key step — 'a step where the usual way of doing it goes wrong in this environment, with an error or silently, and only running the commands reveals it' (sec. 3.3) — knows the set $R_s$ of results that exist only after it (eq. 7), and marks the key-step commands in $\sigma$ with comments 'so that they can be removed mechanically' (App. F); the replays in Table 8 then verify that the verifier sees 598 of 604 key steps. That is a model-free record of which steps force an observation, written by the thing that built the task. The paper uses it to validate the checks, never as a depth measure: the number of verifier-visible key steps per task (at least $k$, 3-6) is never reported next to $D$ (10-80 and above), so the gap between 'the steps we deliberately made unanticipatable' and 'the turns our cheap models needed' is unmeasured — 44 of 54 solved tasks have $D \geq 40$ with at most six designed key steps, and the text attributes the rest to waiting, reading and recovery (sec. 4.2) without counting it. Hindsight is also unused: a passing run at cap $D$ is a full trajectory $(a_1, o_1, \dots)$ in which one can read, turn by turn, whether $a_t$ references anything in $o_{t-1}$; the paper reads from these trajectories only the command-line ratio (1.06 times an uncapped run) and the output-token ratio at $T = 1$ (1.98 times on $D = 1$ tasks; App. D). For the six audited datasets no construction-time record exists, so $D$ is the only instrument and the 333 never-solved tasks are blank. Inference (ours, not the paper's): a construction-time depth count (verifier-visible key steps, or the longest chain of segments linked through $R_s$) placed next to $D$ on the same 105 tasks would calibrate the ruler and say how much of $D \geq 40$ is task and how much is model and harness; a per-turn dependency read of the capped passing trajectories would attribute each turn to task, model or harness; and re-measuring a fixed task set with a third, stronger merger would give the size of the one-sided model bias the paper only signs.
occupies: Published: the work / depth decomposition of terminal-task length imported from parallel computing ($W^{*}$ as fewest lines with the state known, $D^{*}$ as fewest rounds over the states the instruction leaves open); the turn-capped estimation protocol ($D$ = smallest stated cap under which one of two runs of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash or GLM-5.3-Flash passes, caps 1 to 80, in terminus-2); the audit of 734 sampled tasks from TMax, FACET, SETA, RST, TB2 and TW with the findings that 278 of 296 solved synthetic tasks (94%) have $D \leq 3$, that uncapped turn counts are several times $D$, that $D$ predicts public pass rates controlling for $W$ ($-0.31$ / $-0.49$) while $N$ does not ($+0.06$), that generation-time difficulty labels correlate $-0.07$ to $-0.11$ with pass rates, and that TB2 author ratings track $D$ ($+0.55$); the Depth segmented-generation pipeline (carry out, then write; key steps; verifier conditions $V_s(e_{s-1}) = 0$ and $V_s(\tilde{\sigma}_s(e_{s-1})) = 0$; names in the instruction, fixes not; replay acceptance) with its check library (Table 7) and the 105-task dataset (median $D$ 40, $W$ 315, frontier pass@1 at most 47%); the merged-instruction and same-seed-environment controls; the compaction-aware SFT cut (sec. 3.5, App. J) and the Qwen3-8B gains on TB2.1 and TBLite; and the recommendation that 'builders of benchmarks and training data report depth alongside work' (sec. 5). Not claimed in the text: a model-free or construction-time depth measure, a $D$ for tasks no model passes, a bound on how far a stronger model lowers $D$, any RL result, or a comparison of SFT on deep vs shallow tasks at equal sample count.

neighbors.title: Tmax: A simple recipe for terminal agents
neighbors.trick: Generate terminal environments in bulk from a taxonomy with difficulty control, personas and verifier diversification, then RL-train 2B-27B open models outcome-only to 33% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 at 9B (abstract fetched via the arXiv API); cited here as generating tasks 'in bulk with controlled difficulty' and reporting 16.3 mean turns, while the audit finds all 94 solved of its 100 sampled tasks pass within three turns (100% $D \leq 3$, median $D$ 1, median $W$ 58; Table 1) and its hardest level almost never passed (1 of 59 with released Gemini runs, App. C).

neighbors.title: Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
neighbors.trick: Start from verified seed tasks and, over fifteen rounds, extend the reference solution, realign verifier and instruction, validate in a fresh sandbox and reuse the result as the next seed, growing median solutions from 67 to 374 lines and dropping DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 from 90% to 2.5% (abstract fetched via the arXiv API); cited here as extending 'verified tasks over recursive rounds, each perturbing the environment and rewriting the instruction and verifier', the deepest synthetic set audited (200 sampled, 58 solved, 21% $D \geq 5$) yet with 79% of solved tasks at $D \leq 3$ and median $W$ 119 — the paper's exhibit that recursion adds work.

neighbors.title: SETA: Scaling Environments for Terminal Agents
neighbors.trick: Scale terminal environments for agent training with difficulty levels set at generation (abstract not fetched; described from this paper's text only); cited here with TMax as generating tasks 'in bulk with controlled difficulty' whose labels 'record what was requested rather than what models find hard'; audit: 100 sampled, 91 solved, 98% $D \leq 3$, median $D$ 1, median $W$ 25 (Table 1), the CAMEL harness with a 30-turn limit and 1,000-character output in its own paper (Table 3).

neighbors.title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
neighbors.trick: Compose skill packages into terminal scenarios while keeping the source intent and an executable state (abstract not fetched; described from this paper's text only); cited here as a method that 'composes skill packages into scenarios' and reports 11.86 mean turns; audit: 210 sampled, 53 solved, 92% $D \leq 3$, median $D$ 2 with the largest synthetic median $W$ at 204 lines (Table 1) — many operations, few forced rounds.

neighbors.title: TerminalWorld: Benchmarking Agents on Real-World Terminal Tasks
neighbors.trick: Build terminal tasks from real terminal recordings with human review (abstract not fetched; described from this paper's text only); cited here as the human-curated set that 'builds tasks from real terminal recordings and has people review them', and the source of most of the 136 seed environments (1,530 packages); audit of the Verified subset: 85 sampled, 68 solved, 90% $D \leq 3$, median $W$ 11, and 35 original tasks paired against the paper's own from the same environments have $D \leq 10$ in 34 and $D = 1$ in 26 (sec. 4.4).

theme_fit.why: benchmark validity with an instrument: a ruler (smallest stated turn cap that passes) that separates work from forced rounds, applied to 734 tasks, showing uncapped turn counts and generation-time labels fail as horizon and difficulty measures while $D$ predicts pass rates controlling for $W$; the ruler's own validity (censoring on unsolved tasks, one-sided model dependence, two-run noise) is the lane's next question

supplies an enabling piece, not a training result: tasks with $D \geq 40$ and a stated cap as a controllable horizon knob, and a compaction-aware SFT cut (runs split where terminus-2 would compress, sec. 3.5, App. J); the only training shown is SFT of Qwen3-8B with no equal-sample shallow-task control and no RL

same words, different problem: context compression appears only as the point at which training samples are cut and restarted from the summary and Q&A (App. J); nothing about what the summary costs is measured
reports minutes and end-of-run tokens per run (Tables 1, 2, 6) and $1.08 generation cost per accepted task, as side columns; no cost structure is analysed

limitations_as_complaints: My depth number is read off whichever cheap models happened to pass under the cap, so when a task comes out at $D = 40$ I cannot say how much is the task and how much is the model or the harness, and I only know that a better merger would push it down, not by how much: 'Unlike the idealized $D^{*}$, $D$ depends on the models, the harness and the single state $e_{0}$, so it is an estimate rather than a bound' (sec. 2); 'a model that merges poorly overestimates the depth' (sec. 3.1).

My audit is blank exactly where depth matters most: a task nobody passes has no depth at all, and my sample was drawn from passed tasks to begin with, so 333 of 734 sampled tasks and the hardest tier of every synthetic set are unmeasured: 'Due to the implementation of the measurement method, a task that no model passes yields no estimate of $D$' (sec. 4.1); 'Only tasks that at least one model passes in the released results are drawn, since a task that no model passes gives no estimate of $D$; in the hardest level of TMax, only 1 of the 59 tasks with released Gemini runs was ever passed' (App. C).

My headline that depth predicts difficulty is measured with two runs per cap by a model that fails more on hard tasks, so part of the correlation can be my own estimator's failures, and I chose not to control for it: 'both runs at a sufficient cap can fail and raise $D$ by a cap; such tasks may also be harder for other models, so this error could produce a correlation between $D$ and difficulty that does not come from depth' (App. E.2); 'We do not control for $R$ instead: a deep task has many steps that can each go wrong, so part of the variation in $R$ may come from depth itself' (App. E.2).
